title: 3-Read Friday #71: Explanations, Modelling, and Curriculum Amnesia
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #71 gathers three posts loosely united by the theme of what actually does the work in good teaching, versus what merely looks like teaching. Dylan Kane argues that explanations are not the central component of explicit instruction; across Direct Instruction, Rosenshine's principles, and the JUMP maths curriculum, the real engine of learning is the questions and tasks students are given, not the teacher's talk. Emma Turner picks up an adjacent thread, arguing that live teacher modelling - drawing, annotating, and narrating expert thinking in real time - is a dying art being quietly displaced by pre-made digital slides, and that this loss undermines the deep pupil understanding that only embodied, in-the-moment modelling can build. Mark McCourt closes the issue with a polemical piece warning that England is about to import Scotland's Curriculum for Excellence under a different name, mistaking vague, skills-over-knowledge rhetoric for genuine curriculum reform. Barton's own editorial voice ties the three together around a shared concern: that teaching's real substance - what students do, and the disciplined thinking behind curriculum design - is at risk of being replaced by surface-level performance.
points: Dylan Kane's core claim: across Direct Instruction, Rosenshine's principles, and the JUMP curriculum, explanation is a minor, obvious component of explicit teaching - the real center is the questions and tasks that get students doing and thinking.

Barton's own addendum to Kane's argument: worked examples and the examples a teacher chooses to model are as important as explanations themselves, reflecting his own shift over a decade toward 'talk less, show more.'

Emma Turner's warning that pre-prepared digital slides have created a 'modelling void' - live, large-scale, narrated teacher modelling engages spatial thinking, gesture, and attention in ways static PowerPoint slides cannot replicate.

Mark McCourt's structural argument that England's curriculum and assessment review is repeating Scotland's Curriculum for Excellence mistake, and that durable reform requires institutions with genuine curricular coherence, not just borrowed rhetoric about knowledge-richness.
A shared thread across all three posts: the danger of mistaking surface signals of good practice (talk, slides, slogans) for the substantive work that actually produces learning or reform.
quotes: A really interesting post from Dylan, arguing that explanations are not as important as the questions and tasks we give students.
I would add the examples we choose to model to Dylan's list - one of the most significant changes in my teaching over the last 10 years is to talk less but show more...
...which leads nicely onto this post by Emma in which she argues that not enough emphasis in teacher CPD is put on the art of modelling.
With the proliferation of prepared, clickable PowerPoints, this central tenet of teaching risks dying out.
Who doesn't love a meaty blog post from Mark? Here, Mark returns to his long-running theme about the 30-year cycle in education, and the dangers facing England at the moment.
